title: How I Built My Portfolio Website with ChatGPT and GitHub
excerpt: An idea, a few free tools, lots of conversations and a surprising number of design revisions.
body:
I've wanted a proper portfolio website for a while. Something I could share with prospective clients, collaborators or anyone who wanted to know a little more about what I do.

But I wanted it to do more than list my skills and projects. I wanted it to reflect the kind of work I'm doing right now, the things I'm exploring and how I want people to experience my work.

At this point in my journey, I'm working as an AI Creative Technologist. My interests sit somewhere between creative storytelling, AI-powered video production and building practical digital experiences. I wanted a website that could bring those different parts of my work together without making everything feel disconnected.

There was just one small consideration: I didn't want to spend money building it. Not yet, anyway.

Starting with an idea, not a template

I started by working with ChatGPT to figure out what I wanted the website to look and feel like. I wasn't interested in a generic portfolio template with stock photographs and the usual professional introduction. I wanted something that felt like me.

We explored the structure, wording, colours, typography and overall visual direction. I wanted something clean, warm and editorial. Professional but not overly corporate. Something that could communicate what I do without sounding like a sales pitch.

My logo became an important reference point. Its cream background, charcoal lettering and terracotta details helped establish the look and feel. Once we had a direction, ChatGPT helped bring the design to life.

I had a lot of opinions. And I wasn't afraid to use them.

Getting a website built was only part of the process. Getting it to look and feel exactly how I imagined was another matter entirely.

I had opinions about almost everything. The headline needed to communicate what I do clearly. My professional title, AI Creative Technologist, needed to stand out in terracotta. The text and portrait in the hero section had to align properly.

And then there were the images. I wanted images that actually communicated the work I do, not random photographs added just to make the website look less empty. We created a warm portrait for the hero section and another showing me working in a home-office setting for the About section.

I also wanted the website to speak to different kinds of visitors, from brands and businesses to coaches, educators, creative teams and development organisations. We created a visual diagram to communicate that, too.

Then came the spacing, section dividers, background colours, image proportions and alignment. There were moments when I would refresh the website, spot something that didn't look quite right and return to ChatGPT with another correction. Sometimes it was a tiny adjustment. Sometimes it meant rethinking an entire section.

I learned that being specific about what you want makes a huge difference. Saying something looks wrong is one thing. Explaining what feels wrong, where it happens and what you would prefer instead makes it much easier to get the result you're after.

From ChatGPT to a live website

I didn't want to pay for a website builder or commit to a monthly subscription while I was still figuring things out. So we settled on a simple combination of tools.

ChatGPT helped with the website design, writing and code. GitHub became the place where the website files were stored and managed. Cloudflare Pages connected to the repository and published the website online.

I could describe what I wanted, review the changes, give feedback and work towards the result without having to write the code myself. There was still some learning involved, particularly around connecting the tools and making sure changes appeared correctly on the live website. But the process was much more approachable than I expected.

And eventually, the website was live.

A few things I took away from the experience

You don't have to know how to do everything yourself. Knowing what you want to achieve, asking the right questions and learning how to use the tools available to you can take you a long way.

AI works best when you bring your own judgement. ChatGPT could generate designs and make changes, but I still had to decide what worked, what didn't and what needed to change. The final direction came from the combination of its capabilities and my own input.

Details matter. The difference between a website that simply works and one that feels thoughtfully put together can come down to seemingly small things: spacing, alignment, image choices, colours and words.

And finally, you don't have to wait until everything is perfect or until you have a big budget to start putting your work out there.

So, what's next?

This website is a reflection of what I'm doing and exploring right now. It brings my work together in one place and gives people a better sense of the person behind it.

But I know my interests will continue to evolve. My professional title may change. I may explore new tools, build different things or find myself fascinated by something completely unexpected. And that's perfectly fine.

For now, I'm happy to have a little corner of the internet that feels like mine. A place to share what I create, what I learn and the things I'm curious about.

One idea at a time. One experiment at a time. And, apparently, one website revision at a time.
